prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing neutral-atom clocks to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks (B059) with Katori and Ye as my final position; my configuration is unchanged from round 1 and round 2 has only sharpened the reasons. Four of eight members now prefer it with identical names, and seven of eight either prefer it or list it as an alternative, but I do not rest the case on counts. The scientific core is that a clock transition in a neutral atom can be held in an optical lattice at the magic wavelength so that Doppler, recoil and first-order Stark shifts are removed at the same time while a very large number of atoms is interrogated in parallel. That was a new idea, not a refinement, and the part I trust most as a theorist working next to experimentalists is that the physical detail is understood: lattice light shifts, higher-order polarisability, blackbody radiation and collisional effects are each measured and modelled. The result is robust across laboratories, since several independent groups reach and compare clocks at the 1e-18 level, and it has opened a regime that nothing else reaches, namely millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, many-body physics in a clock, and sharper limits on drifting constants and dark matter. On the chair's distinctness question my answer is that the 2005 comb prize gave the means to count optical cycles and the 2012 prize honoured control of single trapped quantum systems. The lattice clock is a different architecture that trades single-ion control for many neutral atoms, and the citation should be written around the magic-wavelength lattice itself and the accuracy it enabled, with no reference to combs or to optical clocks in general. On credit, Katori's proposal and first demonstrations and Ye's drive to the accuracy and many-body frontier are separable, and for the Ye part I would anchor the credit in the strontium lattice-clock accuracy work and not in comb-linked contributions. On maturity, I read the pending redefinition of the second as a sign of maturity, because it is the metrology community's own judgement that the clocks agree well enough, and not as a reason to wait.
statement.case_against: The distinctness argument is the real cost and I do not want to wave it away. A sceptic can say that Hall and Hansch gave the tool, Wineland gave the quantum-control paradigm, and the lattice clock is the best application of both, and that Ye in particular is associated with the comb and cavity-stabilisation lineage that is already honoured. I cannot fully settle the priority record of 2003 to 2006 from memory: Lemonde, Gill, Bloom, Ludlow, Takamoto and others made real contributions, and I would welcome a primary-record check by outside reviewers before the final vote. If that check showed that the first realisation and the accuracy frontier cannot be divided between Katori and Ye as I believe, I would reconsider the pair. A secondary cost is that the main societal payoff, a redefined second, geodesy and dark-matter results, is still ahead. I accept that the committee is honouring a demonstrated capability and a measurement regime, not a delivered application.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether Katori's proposal and first strontium demonstrations are his alone and whether Ye's contribution is an original advance or a later, more precise version, and she says the prize is not for the second discoverer who did it better.
responses.response: I share that principle and think it is the right test for this pairing. My answer is that Ye's contribution goes beyond better numbers: bringing the clock to 1e-18 required new understanding of the lattice-induced shifts, the many-body and collisional behaviour of the atoms, and the coherence of the interrogation laser, and that is why the clock became a precision instrument and not a demonstration. I still agree that this must be checked against the primary record. I would not accept a citation that implies Ye is credited for comb work already honoured, and I would support asking outside reviewers to confirm the 2003 to 2006 chronology, including the Paris work of Lemonde and others, before we fix the two names.

responses.point: Kroll says Ye's group results are partly built on the comb and cavity-stabilisation work of the Hall lineage, and he asks whether the lattice clock is a distinct achievement and not a continuation of the already honoured line.
responses.response: I think your point about Ye's lineage is correct as history and is the reason the citation must be explicit. My answer is that building on a toolbox does not make a result a continuation of it: the 2005 prize is not a reason to exclude every later use of combs, any more than Wineland's prize excludes ion clocks being surpassed. What matters is whether the new result is a new physical regime, and I think the neutral-atom lattice clock is. I note that your Hall-lineage connection is a disclosure for the committee and not a disqualification in my view, and I would not object to your participating if you are comfortable and the chair agrees. I would still prefer that the priority check be done by someone outside our circle.

responses.point: Lindroth says that agreement of independent clocks at the 1e-18 level is exactly the maturity the committee looks for, and she keeps circuit QED as her first alternative.
responses.response: I accept your maturity argument and have adopted it, and your point that theory and experiment agree closely carries weight with me too, since the systematic shifts are computed and then measured. We differ little on B013 as an alternative. Where I want to be careful is your remark that you rank this first partly because it lies in your own field and you may overvalue the elegance of precision; I would apply the same discipline to myself on circuit QED, which is why I am asking colleagues to treat my B013 assessments as discounted and not as decisive.

responses.point: Eriksson alone prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B034) as a prediction followed by experimental discovery of correlated and superconducting states, and argues the prize would be for the phases and not for the pairing mechanism.
responses.response: Your argument that the prize can honour the existence of the phases without a settled mechanism is reasonable, and I would apply the same standard to the lattice clock, where the instrument is also understood in detail. Where I still differ is on maturity. Eight years is short, device and sample dependence is still large, and Cao and Fatemi, whose experiments first saw the states, sit outside the Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero trio. I keep B034 as my second alternative and expect it to be a strong candidate in a later year, but I cannot support it as the single best choice this year. I defer to you and to the condensed-matter members on whether the superconducting phase is as reproducible as you describe.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, prefers IceCube (B043) as a new observational window, states its attribution and source-level maturity reservations himself, and asks that I not lead the committee's judgement on credit in B013.
responses.response: That request is entirely appropriate and I will follow it: I will not argue for B013 or take part in credit decisions on it, and I welcome outside review of that case. On IceCube I defer to the astroparticle members since it is outside my expertise, and I would only say that your own reservation about three names and the Baikal and AMANDA history is the same kind of attribution cost I find hard to accept in a collaboration prize. If the committee were to place B043 and B059 side by side, my preference for B059 would be because two names with a separable record are more defensible than three with open claims.

responses.point: Mehlig asks whether the distinctness argument against circuit QED survives, and prefers topological insulators (B016) because the mechanism is identified and understood, while conceding the overlap with the 2016 prize and the Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Hasan claims.
responses.response: I do not think the distinctness argument for B013 survives well enough this year, which is why I have moved off it, and I would not say that the Z2 classification and circuit QED are on equal footing as organising principles. For B016 I agree the physics is mature and I would rate it highly, but I put it behind B059 for the reasons you give yourself: the 2016 prize already covers much of the conceptual foundation, and the Hasan and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang claims make any three-name set contestable. If the lattice clock priority check fails, B016 would be among the candidates I would look at again, though I defer to you and Eriksson on the condensed-matter judgement.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts lattice clocks as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether the citation wording can state that distinction.
Whether the primary record of 2003 to 2006 supports Katori and Ye alone against Lemonde, Gill, Bloom, Ludlow, Takamoto and others; this should be checked by outside reviewers.
Whether Ye's credit is best anchored in the strontium lattice-clock accuracy work and not in the comb-linked work already honoured.
Whether the committee reads the pending redefinition of the second as maturity or as a reason to wait; I read it as maturity.
How the committee weighs the 2025 circuit prize against B013, which I cannot judge impartially.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology (WACQT) and work on superconducting circuits and microwave quantum optics at Chalmers, so I recuse myself from advocacy on circuit QED (B013) and from credit decisions on it, as the chair has asked. WACQT also hosts quantum-sensing work led by a colleague on this committee, but I have no personal, institutional or funding connection to Katori, Ye or their groups, and I see no conflict on B059. I flag that the other WACQT-linked connections, such as Chalmers hosting 2025 laureates as guest researchers, do not bear on B059.
